🧠 Crypto News Brief: Risk appetite roared back after a dovish nudge from the Fed pushed Bitcoin above $81,000 and torched over $415M in shorts. Beneath the rally, Washington's crypto agenda wobbles and sanctioned hackers keep probing DeFi's plumbing. 🚀 Bitcoin Reclaims $81K as Fed's Waller Signals Rate Pause Bitcoin surged nearly 6% to top $81,000 for the first time since May after Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he could support holding rates steady this month. The dovish tilt cut September hike odds from roughly 63% to about 50%, dragged the dollar index below 99, and triggered a short squeeze that liquidated more than $415 million in bearish bets. Ether, XRP and BNB rallied alongside as risk appetite returned. Read full story → ⚖️ SEC Proposes First Transfer-Agent Overhaul in 40 Years The SEC unveiled its first major rewrite of transfer-agent rules since the early 1980s, explicitly recognizing blockchain records and tokenized securities inside federal market plumbing. The proposal modernizes registration, recordkeeping, cybersecurity and asset-safeguarding standards, and could let distributed ledgers serve as official records of share ownership. A 60-day public comment window opens once the rule hits the Federal Register. More details → 🏛️ Clarity Act on Life Support as Senate Vote Looms Crypto's flagship market-structure bill, the Clarity Act, enters September with slim odds of passing, and many industry insiders are now resigned that it is dead for 2026. The bill would split oversight between the SEC and CFTC and set registration and anti-money-laundering requirements. Even if it fails, executives note the SEC, CFTC and OCC have already turned markedly friendlier under Trump. Read more → 🟠 Strategy Ends 10-Week Pause, Buys $370M in Bitcoin Michael Saylor's Strategy resumed accumulation after a 10-week hiatus, scooping up 4,603 BTC for about $370 million at an average price of $80,318. The purchase lifts total holdings to 845,050 BTC, cementing the firm's lead as the largest corporate Bitcoin holder by a wide margin. Saylor teased the buy with a familiar weekend "We're ₿ack" post before Monday's disclosure. Dear professionals, we are pleased to share the August edition of the PFI Monthly Research Report. This issue explores key themes shaping financial markets, corporate finance, Czech M&A and private equity — with a common thread running through it: the growing gap between compelling stories and disciplined investment returns. In this issue, we have prepared for you: • PFI Monthly research report including an interview with Julia Cillikova, Executive Director Supervision and Financial Consumer Protection Department at National Bank of Slovakia • Financial markets – The AI boom through the lens of capital cycle theory, arguing that high returns attract capital until new capacity erodes margins; a case that 60/40 is not a neutral allocation but an implicit bet on the inflation regime; an analysis of the S&P 500’s Shiller CAPE reaching 41.18, its second-highest reading in ~155 years; and why the 10-year US Treasury yield has risen toward 4.7% as US government debt surpasses USD 40tn. • Corporate finance – Capital allocation 101 (Part I): a clear map of where corporate capital comes from and the main routes to deploy it — organic investment, M&A, buybacks and dividends — and why each choice creates or destroys value. • Czech M&A – Pekárny Srnín’s agreed acquisition of PAC Hořovice, a transaction implying a value of around CZK 1bn that would mark the largest Czech bakery deal since 2019 and accelerate sector consolidation. • Private equity – Building beats buying: add-on acquisitions now account for roughly three-quarters of US buyout activity, making operational integration — not deal access — the real differentiator. 👉 Read the full edition to explore all insights in detail. We would also like to warmly thank partners of the Prague Finance Institute: CERGE-EI, Deník e15, KPMG Czech Republic, Conseq Investment Management, a.s., Oriens, PPF Group, TARPAN Partners, BHM group, RSJ Investments, ARETE, X Production s.r.o., White & Case LLP, Cushman & Wakefield, House of Julius Meinl Limited, Datasite and EKP Advisory. Without them our activities would not be possible. Best regards, Prague Finance Institute

Welcome back! Today: Nvidia funding its own customers, OpenAI's agent that uses software like a person, a forecasting model that needs no training and ChatGPT, Claude and Grok all offline at once In today's Atlas Newsletter: Who funds Nvidia's customers? Nvidia may put $2.5 billion into Thinking Machines Lab, which has already committed to a gigawatt of Nvidia infrastructure. What happens when AI stops needing an API? GPT-6 Astra uses the same screens your employees use, from CRM records to CAD tools. Can one model forecast anything? Google's TimesFM-3 makes zero-shot predictions across interconnected signals, with no per-dataset training. What happens when three rivals share one dependency? ChatGPT, Claude and Grok all went down Thursday morning, and the common thread points somewhere boring. PS: Want to collaborate with the biggest GTM engine and distribution moat for AI companies? You can feature your tool with us and reach millions Nvidia is funding the companies that buy its chips Nvidia may invest $2.5 billion in Thinking Machines Lab, the AI startup founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati. The startup is also reportedly raising at least $1 billion at a valuation of around $40 billion. The detail that explains the deal: Thinking Machines Lab has already committed to using at least 1 gigawatt of Nvidia's Vera Rubin infrastructure. So Nvidia could invest in the company, and part of that money may eventually come back to Nvidia through hardware purchases. This isn't new. Nvidia has made similar investments in OpenAI, Anthropic, cloud companies and AI infrastructure startups. It has backed more than 100 startups in the past two years. The strategy is simple: Nvidia needs AI companies to keep buying more compute, so investing in them helps secure future demand for its chips. The concern is circularity. If Nvidia invests in a company that then spends heavily on Nvidia hardware, it becomes harder to tell how much demand is truly independent. And Nvidia is spending aggressively across the AI ecosystem, including the reported $12.93 billion Hugging Face acquisition and the $1 billion Poolside deal. Nvidia now sells the infrastructure behind AI and funds the companies that need it. The enterprise deal is ready. Is your SOC 2? The fastest-growing startups get compliant early, before the enterprise contract shows up asking for it.  That's where Vanta comes in. Used by 16,
